title: what your grandmother was actually doing
hook: Krishna's poor friend Sudama brings a bundle of rice; why a flower and a cup of water make a whole puja
tomorrow: the thing that's yours to do

segments.voice: Yesterday: karma. Your line was what you do, you become. Week two starts at home, with an old friend and a bundle of rice. Day eight.

Two boys once studied under the same teacher: Krishna, a prince, and a poor brahmin boy remembered as Sudama. Years later Krishna is a king in Dwaraka, and Sudama's family is going hungry. His wife begs him: go and see your old friend. He has nothing to bring, so she begs four handfuls of flattened rice from the neighbors, and he ties them into his worn cloth. At the palace, Krishna runs to hug him, washes his feet, and seats him on his own bed. Then he asks: what did you bring me? Sudama is too ashamed to hand over cheap rice. So Krishna finds it himself, pulls it loose, and eats a handful with joy.
screen: `TWO BOYS, ONE TEACHER.` → `A BUNDLE OF CHEAP RICE.` → `WHAT DID YOU BRING ME?` → `KRISHNA EATS IT WITH JOY.`

segments.voice: This old story holds today's word: puja, the way Hindus worship God with their hands. Before Krishna takes the rice, he says a line many Hindus know by heart, from the Bhagavad Gita: whoever offers me a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, with devotion, I accept it. In Sanskrit it begins: patram pushpam phalam toyam. Nothing on that list costs much. What God receives is the devotion, bhakti, the heart tied up in the gift. Now look at a home puja. Many follow the steps of welcoming an honored guest, the way Krishna welcomed Sudama: a seat, water for the feet, water to sip. Then a flower, incense, a waved lamp, a bell, and food. Afterward the food comes back as prasad, a gift from God, shared and eaten. A shrine can be a whole room or one shelf with a picture and a lamp. That's the teaching: in Hinduism, the size of the offering was never the point. A marigold and a cup of water, offered with love, is a whole puja. What you're really bringing is yourself: your care, your attention, for a few minutes given to God. So a grandmother at that shelf before the kettle goes on isn't only keeping a custom. Like Sudama, she's bringing what she has, and it's enough.
screen: `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER` · `THE DEVOTION IS THE GIFT` · `AN HONORED GUEST, THEN PRASAD` · `THE SIZE WAS NEVER THE POINT` · then, large: `ATTENTION IS AN OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, the smallest puja there is. If you have a shrine or a picture of God, set one thing before it: a flower, a cup of water, a piece of fruit. If you don't, set something you love in front of you. Look at it first. Then offer it with both hands, and give it your full attention. If you pray, say silently: this is for you. If you don't, just let one thing have all of you for a while. The bell holds the time.
Puja. Worship with the hands: water, a flower, a flame, food, offered with devotion. Eighth word.
Your line: attention is an offering. Krishna wanted the rice for the love tied up in it. Give one thing today your whole attention, and you've given what matters. Day eight.

screen: `DAY 8 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE THING THAT'S YOURS TO DO.`

howItsDone: At a home shrine, a devotee may offer water, flowers, incense, a waved lamp and food, ring a bell, and then share the food as prasad; temple priests perform puja in the same spirit on a larger scale.

fork.reveal: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, offered with devotion, is accepted. Krishna took Sudama's handful of rice the same way. the cost was never the point.

original.note: Sanskrit: honor, worship; care offered to God, often through the senses.

trapdoor: what you thought: worship, something formal, expensive and far away.
what it means: a small, hands-on act of love: water, flower, flame, bell, food, given back as prasad.
what a scholar hears: Bhagavata Purana 10.80–81: Krishna repeats patram pushpam phalam toyam (Gita 9.26) and takes Sudama's rice. the devotion is what's accepted.
